info.headline.lede: The app makes two choices about where the money comes from on its own, each measured here on {households} simulated households: Roth conversion tax {funding}, and each household draws in whichever of Pro-rata or Tax-optimized sustains more spending. Against every combination of six withdrawal orders and five conversion policies, the median household can't do more than {median} better. The biggest remaining gaps come from converting more than the app does, for early retirees with most of their money in Tax Deferred accounts.

info.headline.fundingGain: average gain in sustainable spend from paying conversion tax out of the conversion instead of only from Brokerage

info.tested.profile: Each household got a random but reproducible profile: retiring at 50–70 between 2026 and 2032 for 20–40 years, $300k–$5M split across Tax Deferred, Roth and Brokerage (0–90% embedded gains), Social Security of $0–$4,500 a month starting at 62–70, an inheritance half the time, and one of the four investment scenarios.
info.tested.method: Every combination of a withdrawal order and a Roth conversion policy (defined below) ran on the same {paths} market paths for each household, so every difference on this page is paired: same household, same markets, only the strategy changed. For each path the lab found the largest annual spend it survives (to $100); the 82.5% spend — the most spending that survives 82.5% of paths — is read off those break-evens exactly as the Optimal page does, and it's the yardstick throughout. The lab runs the app's own year-by-year engine, and a self-check confirms it survives exactly when the app does.
info.definitions.ordersIntro: Which accounts pay for each year's spending, and in what order.
info.definitions.policiesIntro: After each year's spending, Tax Deferred money is converted to Roth until the year's gross ordinary income reaches the policy's line.
info.definitions.col.convertsUntil: Converts until gross ordinary income reaches
info.definitions.zeroRateAlternative: , or {amount} minus the gains already realized that year, if lower
info.definitions.note.grossIncome: Gross ordinary income includes taxable Social Security and the year's Tax Deferred withdrawals. The lines are inflated each year like the tax brackets, and a year already past its line converts nothing.
info.definitions.note.appPicks: The app picks the line for each household among {c0}, {c1}, {c3} and {c4} (see How the app chooses); {c2} and {c5} are lab-only.
info.definitions.note.gate: Conversions ignore the 59½ gate, and converted dollars count as Roth basis, which can be spent at any age.
info.definitions.note.irmaa: Big conversions raise Medicare premiums later. From 65, the model charges the Medicare IRMAA surcharge set by income two years earlier (2026 tiers, starting above $109,000 of MAGI for a single filer and $218,000 for a married couple, who each pay it; inflated each year) on top of spending. The first two years of retirement pay none, as after a work-stoppage appeal.
info.definitions.note.funding: Where the conversion's tax comes from is set by the funding rule below.
info.definitions.note.fundingApp: Where the conversion's tax comes from is set by the funding rule below — the app uses {code}.
info.definitions.fundingIntro: Where a Roth conversion's tax comes from. Paying out of the conversion is the same, dollar for dollar, as withholding from Tax Deferred or paying from Roth afterwards, so those aren't separate rules.
info.funding.intro: The Strategy Lab found that paying a conversion's tax only by selling Brokerage stalls conversions once Brokerage runs low, which hurts early retirees most. Every funding rule was run on the same {households} households and markets, with the 12% fill ({c1}), compared with Tax-optimized paying only from Brokerage ({baseline}, the app before this change). The rule for adopting one: the highest average gain with its 95% interval above zero, a median of at least zero, and losses (worse than −0.5%) in at most 5% of households.
info.funding.byAge: Tax-optimized with each rule, by retirement age
info.orders.intro: Which accounts pay for each year's spending is the app's choice, not an input. Each withdrawal order was run with the app's conversion policy and conversion tax funding, and compared with the best order for the same household. An order can be the app's one fixed rule if it's within 0.5% of the best in at least 95% of households and no household type falls short by more than 1% on average.
info.orders.noneQualifies: No single order qualifies, so the app picks the order for each household.
info.conversion.heading: How far to convert
info.conversion.intro: The app also picks how far each year's Roth conversion goes (the conversion policies above), together with the order: for each household it tries Pro-rata and Tax-optimized with no conversions, the 12% fill, the top of the 22% bracket and the top of the 24% bracket, and keeps the pair that sustains the spending best. Below, each way of picking against the best of every combination the lab ran for the same household.
info.conversion.col.picker: Chosen by the Scenario runner's picker
info.conversion.picker: The Scenario runner picks with a quicker test — survival at the entered spend on 200 market paths — so it was run on every household at its ideal spend: it lands within 0.5% of the ideal pick for {share} of households (average shortfall {shortfall}). The Optimal page uses the fuller search.

info.direct.heading: Pro-rata vs Tax-optimized
info.direct.intro: For most households the two orders are close once Roth conversions are on; the median household sees a difference of a few hundredths of a percent.
info.direct.explanation: Without conversions, Pro-rata beats Tax-optimized in about half of households by a small margin: spreading Tax Deferred draws evenly over the whole retirement keeps more of them in low brackets than a strict order. With the 12% fill on, that advantage mostly disappears, because conversions fill the cheap brackets every year under either order.
info.optimal.intro: The Optimal page's default inputs and asset mix, run through its optimizer with the behavior before this change (Tax-optimized, conversion tax only from Brokerage) and with the app's current choices. Monthly spend in today's dollars at the recommended Social Security age.
info.grid.intro: Average change in the 82.5% spend versus the Tax-optimized baseline. Wins and losses count households where the difference is more than ±0.5% (smaller gaps are within the $100 search precision). A few early retirees pull the averages up; the median is the typical household.
info.grid.noHarvesting: Plus Tax-optimized without 0% gain harvesting ({code}): {average} average, median {median}, wins {wins}, loses {loses}.
info.whoLoses.intro: The gap between the Tax-optimized baseline and the best of all combinations, by household type. The last column is Pro-rata with the 12% fill versus the Tax-optimized baseline.
info.whoLoses.winners: In the {households} households where some combination beat the Tax-optimized baseline by more than 3%, the winners were: {winners}.
info.case.gate: Before 59½ the model locks Tax Deferred money and Roth gains; only Brokerage and Roth basis can be spent. Roth conversions are the way through: converted dollars count as Roth basis, so they can be spent right away.
info.case.callout: Tax-optimized is gains-first: it sells Brokerage while the gains are taxed at 0%. Those gains fill the 0% band, and the 12% fill ({c1}) stops conversions short rather than push them to 15%. Converting less means less new Roth basis, so when Brokerage runs out before 59½ there isn't enough accessible money — even with Tax Deferred still full. Pro-rata spends some Roth basis alongside Brokerage, realizes fewer gains and keeps converting. This is why the app picks the order for each household rather than always using one.

info.pageDefaults.intro: Retire 1/1/2027 at 57, $950k Tax Deferred, $20k Roth, $400k Brokerage (half gains), a $1M inheritance in year 10, and $2,750 a month from 62. Monthly 82.5% spend in today's dollars, with the change versus the Tax-optimized baseline.
info.conclusions.withinYear: Tax-optimized works as intended within a year. Its single-year decisions are exactly tax-minimal.
info.conclusions.funding: Conversion tax comes out of the conversion. Compared with paying it only by selling Brokerage, this raises the 82.5% spend by {average} on average (95% interval {from} to {to}), mostly for early retirees whose conversions used to stall; it lowers it by more than 0.5% for {lossShare} of households.
info.conclusions.orderPick: The app picks the withdrawal order for each household. Neither Pro-rata nor Tax-optimized is best everywhere; the better of the two is within 0.5% of the best of all six orders for {share} of households.
info.conclusions.conversionsMatter: Roth conversions matter. Without them, Tax-optimized's 82.5% spend is {average} lower on average and at least {worst} lower for the worst-hit 5% of households — early retirees who need the bridge to 59½.
info.conclusions.conversionPick: The app picks how far to convert. Converting to the top of the 22% bracket ({c3}) lowers the typical household's spend (median {median}) but helps some a great deal{heavy}, so the app chooses the line with the order. Picking both is within 0.5% of the best of everything tried for {both} of households, against {orderOnly} when only the order was picked.
info.conclusions.conversionPickHeavy: (an average of {average} for households with 75%+ in Tax Deferred)
info.conclusions.harvesting: 0% gain harvesting makes no measurable difference ({average} on average).
info.conclusions.earlyConversion: Converting heavily early doesn't raise safe spending. Conversion lines that change over the years add at most {added} out of sample. The app keeps one line per household, chosen so the household doesn't run out of money rather than to leave the largest balance when markets go well.
info.early.intro: A common idea is to convert as much as possible to Roth in the first years of retirement, before Social Security and required minimum distributions (RMDs) add to taxable income, so more of the portfolio grows tax-free. The Strategy Lab tested it with {schedules} conversion schedules whose line changes over the years — for example, the top of the 24% bracket until Social Security starts, then the 12% fill. Each switches on something a household knows that year: its age, whether Social Security or RMDs have started, or how much of its money is still Tax Deferred. The app instead picks one line per household for its whole retirement.
info.early.method: Each rule was chosen on {fit} households and judged on {holdout} others, and every household's pick was made on one set of 200 simulated markets and measured on a different 200 — the way the app picks before a household's real future arrives. To be adopted, a rule had to raise the 82.5% spend by at least {bar} on average, with its 95% interval above zero and no household type worse off than {worst} on average.
info.early.rule.plusOne: The app's pick, also offered 1 schedule
info.early.rule.plusMany: The app's pick, also offered {count} schedules
info.early.rule.plusAll: The app's pick, also offered every schedule
info.early.rule.tree: A decision tree on household facts
info.early.verdict: No rule passed. Offering every schedule beside the app's own four lines adds {added} on average (95% interval {from} to {to}) — real, but far below the bar — and one schedule for every household loses {single}.
info.early.verdictAdopted: At least one rule passed the bar (highlighted).
info.early.tradeOffs.heading: What converting heavily early does
info.early.tradeOffs.intro: Each household is run at the 82.5% spend of the app's usual line ({baseline}, the 12% fill), comparing the after-tax money left at the end, in today's dollars, in its strong markets (the 90th-percentile market) and its weaker ones (the 25th percentile). The figures are the median household's difference from {baseline} and the share of households the policy leaves with more. Tax Deferred left over counts at 78% of its value and Brokerage gains at 85%, as everywhere in the lab.

info.early.why.heading: Why
info.early.why.goal: The goal is not running out of money. The app looks for the most a household can spend that still survives 80–85% of simulated markets. That margin is what lets a household sleep at night: the plan holds in all but the worst 15–20% of markets, not just in average ones.
info.early.why.weakMarkets: The markets that decide survival are the weak ones. A conversion pays tax now to save tax later. In a weak market — especially one that falls early — the money sent to the IRS early is gone exactly when the portfolio needs it, and the tax it was meant to save often never comes due: Tax Deferred is mostly spent before RMDs would push it into higher brackets.
info.early.why.strongMarkets: In some strong markets, converting more would leave more. When markets do well, Tax Deferred grows large, RMDs push it into higher brackets, and converting early pays off: converting heavily left more after-tax money in strong markets for {share} of households. The app knowingly gives that up. Its goal is to not run out of money, not to leave the largest balance in markets that go well — a subtle but very important distinction.{median}
info.early.why.strongMedian: (For the median household, converting heavily left no more even in strong markets: {range}.)
info.early.why.edge: Where a plan is closest to the edge, converting heavily leaves much less. In each household's weaker markets, the median household's after-tax money left changed by {range}.
info.early.why.pick: The app already adapts how far to convert. Its per-household pick among four lines (none, the 12% fill, the top of 22%, the top of 24%) captures nearly all of what a changing line could add.
info.reproduce.notes: Writes CSVs and summary.json to MonteCarloSimulation.StrategyLab/output/, and with --publish updates this page's data. The same seed gives the same numbers. After-tax ending wealth values Tax Deferred at 78% and Brokerage gains at 85%. Seed {seed}, {paths} paths per household, published {published}.

lab.def.W1: Each year's spending comes from every accessible account in proportion to its balance (Tax Deferred and Roth gains only from 59½).
lab.def.W2: The app's order. Brokerage while its gains are taxed at 0%, then Tax Deferred up to the start of the 22% bracket (or less, to keep those gains at 0%), then more Brokerage at 15/20%, then more Tax Deferred, then Roth. Any 0% capital gains room left over is harvested.
lab.def.W3: The earlier tax-optimized order: Tax Deferred up to the start of the 22% bracket, then Brokerage, then more Tax Deferred, then Roth.
lab.def.W4: The conventional rule of thumb: Brokerage until it's empty, then Tax Deferred, then Roth.
lab.def.W5: Drain Tax Deferred first: Tax Deferred until it's empty, then Brokerage, then Roth.
lab.def.W6: Each chunk of spending ($1,000, or 1/25 of the year's need if larger) comes from whichever of Tax Deferred and Brokerage adds the least tax this year; Roth last.
lab.def.W2nh: W2 without the 0% capital gains harvesting, to isolate what harvesting adds.
lab.def.C1: Fills the 12% bracket: up to the start of the 22% bracket, or lower when more ordinary income would push the gains already realized this year out of the 0% capital gains band.
lab.def.C2: Up to the start of the 22% bracket, even if that moves this year's 0% gains to 15%.
lab.def.C3: Up to the top of the 22% bracket.
lab.def.C4: Up to the top of the 24% bracket.
lab.def.C5: Up to the top of the 22% bracket, but stopping where the year's income (ordinary plus gains realized so far) would cross the first Medicare IRMAA tier.
lab.def.F0: The conversion's tax is paid only by selling Brokerage; a conversion is scaled down to what Brokerage can pay.
lab.def.F1: The tax always comes out of the converted amount, so less of it reaches Roth.
lab.def.F2: Brokerage pays while it can; the rest comes out of the converted amount, so conversions never stall.
lab.def.F3: Like F2, but before 59½ Brokerage pays only from what it holds beyond the spending still to come before 59½.

gordon.subtitle: Guided setup
gordon.moveHint: Drag to move Gordon, or use the arrow keys. Double-click or press Home to put it back in the corner.
gordon.intro.hello: Hi, I'm Gordon. I'll set up your retirement plan, pick one of the options below.
gordon.ask.birth: First, when were you born? Month and year is enough.
gordon.retry.birth: I didn't catch a birth date. Try something like June 1967 or 6/15/1967.
gordon.ack.birthYearOnly: Got it. I'll use {date}; you can set the exact date on the Demographics tab.
gordon.ack.birthFromAge: Thanks. At {age}, I'll use {date} as your birth month; you can set the exact date on the Demographics tab.
gordon.ask.retire: When do you plan to retire? A date, a year, an age (at 62) or in 3 years all work.
gordon.retry.retire: I need a retirement date from 2026 on, after your birthday and before age 99. Try January 2028 or at 65.
gordon.ack.horizon: I'll plan for {years} years, until you're {age}, and test the plan in 99 simulated markets.
gordon.ask.filing: How will you file your taxes?
gordon.retry.filing: Are you filing single, or married filing jointly?
gordon.ack.married: Married filing jointly: noted. I'll use the joint tax brackets and deduction.
gordon.ask.taxDeferred: Now your savings, one kind at a time. How much is in tax-deferred accounts: 401(k)s, 403(b)s and traditional IRAs?
gordon.ask.roth: How much is in Roth accounts (Roth IRAs and Roth 401(k)s)?
gordon.ask.brokerage: And in regular taxable brokerage accounts: money you've invested outside retirement accounts?
gordon.retry.money: I didn't catch an amount. Try something like 400k, $1.2M or none.
gordon.ask.inheritance: Do you expect an inheritance or another lump sum? If so, about how much?
gordon.ask.inheritanceWhen: In about how many years from now?
gordon.retry.years: How many years from now? A number like 10 works.
gordon.ask.ss: What's your monthly Social Security benefit at full retirement age (67)? It's on your statement at ssa.gov. I'll work out what it pays if you start earlier or later.
gordon.ask.ssMarried: What monthly Social Security do the two of you get combined at full retirement age (67)? It's on your statements at ssa.gov. I'll work out what it pays if you start earlier or later.
gordon.ack.ssDefault: No problem. I'll use {amount} a month at 67 for now; you can change it on the Other Income tab.
gordon.ack.ssYearly: That looks like a yearly amount, so I'll use {amount} a month at 67.
gordon.ask.ssStart: When do you plan to start Social Security? Any age from 62 to 70: starting earlier pays less each month, later pays more.
gordon.retry.ssStart: Social Security can start between 62 and 70. Try 67 or at 70.
gordon.ack.ssStartDefault: I'll use 67, full retirement age for most people, starting in {date}: {amount} a month.
gordon.ask.mix: How would you like your savings invested?
gordon.ask.spending: Last question: how much would you like to spend each month in retirement, in today's dollars?
gordon.retry.spending: I need a monthly amount, like 8,000 or $9.5k, or tap the button to let me find it.
gordon.ack.spendingYearly: That looks like a yearly amount, so I'll use {amount} a month.
gordon.summary.ss: Social Security of {amount} a month from {date}, at {age}
gordon.retry.confirm: Say run to run the plan, or change to fix something first.
gordon.ask.change: What would you like to change?
gordon.retry.change: Pick one of the buttons below.
gordon.running: Running your plan through {runs} simulated markets…
gordon.retry.running: One moment: the simulation is still running.
gordon.result.allSurvived: Good news: your money lasted all {years} years in every one of the {total} simulated markets.
gordon.result.survived: Your money lasted all {years} years in {survived} of {total} simulated markets ({rate}%).
gordon.result.allSurvivedRate: Your money lasted all {years} years in every simulated market.
gordon.result.survivedRate: Your money lasted all {years} years in {rate}% of simulated markets.
gordon.result.median: In a typical market you'd have about {amount} left in {year}, when you're {age} (in future dollars).
gordon.result.medianRunsOut: In a typical market the money runs out around {year}, at about age {age}.
gordon.result.lowerRunsOut: In the weakest 10% of markets the money runs out around {year}, at about age {age}.
gordon.result.lowerHolds: Even in the weakest 10% of markets about {amount} is left in {year}.
gordon.tip.lower: That's below the 80–85% range the app aims for. Spending less than {amount} a month, or retiring later, would make the plan sturdier.
gordon.tip.inRange: That's close to the 80–85% range the app aims for: a cushion against weak markets without spending less than you need to.
gordon.tip.more: That's above the 80–85% range the app aims for, so you may be able to spend more than {amount} a month.
gordon.result.failed: Something went wrong running the plan. Please try again.
gordon.result.invalid: One of the inputs needs fixing first; the form shows which.
gordon.skipped: Skipped: I'll keep what's on the form.
gordon.ask.spendingOptimize: Or I can find it for you: the most you can spend that lasts in about 82.5% of simulated markets, with the best age to start Social Security.
